evidence.note: Hawkins-based treaty limits, earlier cruiser ratings, a proposed unconstrained size hierarchy, and Alaska's classification.

segments.summary: Treaty definitions based on the Hawkins class interrupted the older hierarchy of cruisers and help explain the argument for treating Alaska as a large cruiser.

segments.title: Would faster Renowns replace the Admiral class?
segments.body: More Renowns could be an alternative to building Hood if the earlier class already reached 32 knots. An Admiral-class design would probably still be attempted, however, to see how much further battlecruiser speed could be increased.

evidence.note: Additional Renowns as an alternative, balanced against the incentive to pursue greater Admiral-class speed.

segments.summary: A 32-knot Renown makes more of the same attractive, but leaves an incentive to build an even faster Admiral.
segments.question: Would the Admirals still be built if Renown could already make 32 knots?
segments.answerShort: Probably, because designers would still want to explore a faster ship, although additional Renowns would be a plausible alternative.

segments.title: An American response to Britain's faster capital ships
segments.body: The United States would probably try to build equivalents to the hypothetical fast British capital ships. An American response could include twelve 16-inch guns. The expected design preference would retain somewhat lower speed in exchange for heavier armament.

evidence.note: Hypothetical American preference for heavier guns, potentially twelve 16-inch weapons, at somewhat lower speed.

segments.summary: The expected American response combines heavier armament with somewhat lower speed, potentially using twelve 16-inch guns.
segments.question: How would the United States respond to a British fleet of much more powerful Revenges, Queen Elizabeths, and Admirals?
segments.answerShort: By building equivalents with somewhat lower speed and heavier armament, potentially twelve 16-inch guns.

segments.title: How fast battleships would ease Hood's workload
segments.body: More fast British capital ships would reduce the concentration of demanding duties on Hood. A 28-knot battle line would also change operations in the Mediterranean and elsewhere. Maintaining that speed would make interwar upgrades to the older ships more worthwhile. The result would be one of the faster battle lines available to a navy.

evidence.note: Sharing Hood's duties and preserving a fast battle line through interwar refits.

segments.summary: A larger pool of fast capital ships would share Hood's duties and strengthen the case for modernizing the battle line.
segments.question: Would faster Queen Elizabeths, Revenges, and Renowns give Hood a break from being overworked?
segments.answerShort: Yes, and the larger fast force would also change deployments and interwar modernization decisions.

segments.title: Why battlecruiser classification depends on its contemporaries
segments.body: Battlecruisers can have armor as thick as an earlier generation of battleships while protecting a smaller proportion of the hull. Comparing them only with older ships can therefore obscure the intended distinction. G3 would look more like a fast battleship if built alone, whereas a contemporary N3 would make G3's battlecruiser role easier to recognize. A similar argument could have surrounded Iowa had the larger American battleships planned alongside it also been completed. Speed and belt thickness need to be considered within those contemporary design choices.

evidence.note: Contextual comparisons involving Iowa and unbuilt American battleships, G3 and N3, and armor thickness versus coverage.

segments.summary: G3 and Iowa illustrate how classification changes when a fast ship is compared with the battleships intended to serve alongside it.

segments.title: Why the Admiral class earned its reputation
segments.body: Hood's reputation reflected a period when she was among the largest and most powerful ships in the world. Ships capable of catching her could not outfight her. The wider Admiral design is also judged a promising basis for aircraft carriers, although that remains a design opinion.

evidence.note: Hood's early combination of speed and fighting power and a favorable opinion of the Admirals as potential carriers.

segments.summary: Hood's early combination of speed and fighting power explains why the Admiral class attracted such a strong reputation.
segments.question: Were the Admiral-class battlecruisers overrated?
segments.answerShort: Their reputation had a basis in Hood's early superiority: ships able to catch her could not outfight her.

segments.title: Why fleet availability needs several hulls
segments.body: A rough planning rule treats one ship as a prestige possession, two as intermittently available, three as usually providing one deployable hull, and four as assuring availability. A single carrier can lose its entire operational value during a refit. Maintenance therefore makes the number of ships central to whether a navy can use a capability when it needs it. Hood fits more usefully into this calculation alongside the two Renowns and Tiger as a four-ship battlecruiser force.

evidence.note: The one-through-four hull availability rule and the vulnerability of a single carrier to dry-dock periods.
Hood considered alongside the two Renowns and Tiger as a four-ship battlecruiser force.

segments.summary: One ship is vulnerable to refit cycles, while three or four hulls turn a design into a dependable operational capability.

segments.title: Why more small ships are not automatically cheaper
segments.body: Small ships can be mass-produced, but each still needs engines, command-and-control systems, and weapons. Replacing one large ship with several small ones multiplies those expensive installations. Small wartime designs such as Flower-class corvettes and U-class submarines can also become costly to adapt when their original equipment and arrangements have to be replaced. Repeatedly building replacements for every technological change is unlikely to receive enough funding. Fleet planning therefore needs a balance of sizes and enough room for later changes.

evidence.note: Repeated system costs, the preference for three Hoods over three Renowns, and the cost of adapting small wartime designs.

segments.summary: Several small ships duplicate expensive machinery and combat systems, while tightly packed wartime designs can be difficult to modernize.

segments.title: Furious's 18-inch guns and competing Agincourt hypotheses
segments.body: Furious's single 18-inch mounting is a poor basis for judging what the weapon could do in a larger ship. One hypothesis holds that the gun was shortened to suit Furious and had originally been intended for another design. References to a '15-inch special,' compared with the earlier use of '13.5-inch special' for the 15-inch gun, provide a lead for investigating the unbuilt Agincourt design. Clarke favors six 18-inch guns for that ship, while Drachinifel favors nine or twelve 15-inch guns. These remain competing reconstructions. A six-gun Agincourt at Jutland is then considered as a counterfactual, with the expected effect of its heavy shells kept separate from the unresolved design question.

evidence.note: Furious's mounting limitations, suspected shortening, the '15-inch special' terminology, and the six-gun Agincourt counterfactual.
Clarke favors six 18-inch guns for Agincourt, while Drachinifel favors nine or twelve 15-inch guns.

segments.summary: Furious's installation leads into an unresolved reconstruction of Agincourt, with six 18-inch guns proposed against nine or twelve 15-inch guns.

segments.title: Hood's armor depended on range and hit location
segments.body: Armor comparisons depend on the area and depth of the hull protected as well as nominal thickness. Hood could resist her own 15-inch gun at long range in the protected areas. The same claim does not hold reliably at ordinary engagement ranges. Equal armor thickness on a battleship and battlecruiser also does not mean that the same proportion of each hull is protected.

evidence.note: Hood's resistance to 15-inch fire qualified by engagement range, armor coverage, and the location of a hit.

segments.summary: Hood could resist her own 15-inch gun at long range in protected areas, but equal belt thickness did not give battleship-level coverage everywhere.
segments.question: Was Hood armored against her own 15-inch shells?
segments.answerShort: At long range and in the right protected areas, yes; at ordinary ranges or outside that coverage, not reliably.

segments.title: Hood was intended to lead four ships
segments.body: Hood was intended as the lead ship of a four-ship class. Only one was completed. That outcome makes it easy to remember Hood as an isolated design and overlook the force originally planned.

evidence.note: Intended four-ship Admiral class contrasted with Hood's solitary completion.

segments.summary: Hood's solitary completion obscures the original intention to build four Admiral-class battlecruisers.
segments.question: Why is Hood often remembered as a single ship when she was supposed to lead a class of four?
segments.answerShort: Because only Hood was completed, making that eventual outcome easier to remember than the original four-ship plan.

segments.title: A faster Royal Navy battle line forces foreign redesigns
segments.body: A Royal Navy with numerous 28-knot capital ships would push rival navies to increase their own speeds. British adoption of triple turrets could also encourage American, Japanese, and Italian designers to follow. For Germany, matching a Queen Elizabeth with twelve 15-inch guns in four triple turrets and a speed of 28 knots would require new guns, a new turret, faster machinery, and supporting infrastructure. The combined demands are judged severe enough to threaten German capacity to compete in 1912.

evidence.note: Rival fleets would face pressure to increase speed in response to a numerous fast British battle line.
Triple-turret adoption and the industrial demands of a German response to a hypothetical twelve-gun, 28-knot Queen Elizabeth.

segments.summary: A 28-knot British battle line with triple 15-inch turrets would pressure rivals to develop new machinery, guns, turrets, and supporting infrastructure.
segments.question: How would rivals respond to 28-knot Nelsons and Queen Elizabeths plus faster Hood and Renown classes?
segments.answerShort: They would pursue faster ships and heavier turret arrangements, escalating machinery, armament, and infrastructure costs.

segments.title: Why the United States favored a 35,000-ton limit
segments.body: A 35,000-ton ceiling suited the existing American battle line, and the United States tried to push the Washington negotiations in that direction. Most other navies also lacked a larger ship in service. Only one nation had an operational ship substantially above that size, while other large designs were still building. The American position therefore fitted a situation shared by much of the world's fleet.

evidence.note: American pressure for the limit and the distinction between large ships already in service and those still under construction.

segments.summary: A 35,000-ton treaty ceiling suited the existing American battle line, but almost every navy similarly lacked a larger capital ship already in service.
segments.question: Did the United States push a 35,000-ton treaty limit because it had no larger battleship in service?
segments.answerShort: That helped shape the American position, but most navies also lacked an in-service battleship above the proposed limit.

segments.title: A paper quadruple turret does not establish a working heavy mount
segments.body: A German quadruple-turret proposal for the Dutch raises two separate questions: its calibre and whether a drawing could become a workable installation. The initial recollection is an 11-inch mount, while a viewer proposes 14 inches. That identification remains unresolved after an unsuccessful search, and the possibility of a missed design is acknowledged. Either way, a triple 15-inch turret would impose substantially different weight and stresses from a quadruple 11-inch turret. The example of a Vickers double-stacked quadruple 12-inch design reinforces the distinction between drawing a mount and being able to produce it.

evidence.note: The initial 11-inch recollection and the different engineering demands of a triple 15-inch turret.
A viewer proposes 14 inches, while the search fails to settle the identification and uncertainty is explicitly retained.
A Vickers double-stacked quadruple 12-inch paper design does not establish contemporary production feasibility.

segments.summary: The calibre of a German quadruple-turret proposal remains disputed, while a drawing alone does not establish production feasibility.
segments.question: Didn't Germany offer the Dutch a quadruple-turret design in 1913?
segments.answerShort: A paper proposal is recalled, but its calibre remains disputed. It would not by itself demonstrate the ability to build a triple 15-inch turret.

segments.title: German heavy-gun plans and the space taken by sliding breeches
segments.body: German plans did include 16-inch guns for the H class, although how far their development had progressed remains debated. The fleet otherwise stayed largely with 15-inch guns. A separate objection concerns the space occupied by sliding breech mechanisms. Their engineering advantages are acknowledged as possible, but the practical criticism here is their bulk and the difficulty of operating them in confined arrangements.

evidence.note: Planned H-class 16-inch guns, uncertainty over development, and criticism of the space occupied by sliding breeches.

segments.summary: The H-class plans included 16-inch guns, while the separate criticism of German sliding breeches concerns the space they required.
segments.question: Wouldn't Germany have investigated 14-inch guns because of the treaties?
segments.answerShort: The planned H-class guns were 16-inch, while their development status remains uncertain.

segments.title: Why Royal Sovereign would become the training ship
segments.body: Royal Sovereign is the probable choice for training duty in a six-ship Revenge-class fleet. The oldest ship was normally assigned that role, so service age provides the basis for the choice.

evidence.note: Royal Sovereign provisionally selected because the oldest ship normally became the training ship.

segments.summary: In a six-ship Revenge-class counterfactual, Royal Sovereign is the likely training ship because navies normally assign the oldest hull to that duty.
segments.question: With six Revenge-class battleships, which one would probably become the training ship?
segments.answerShort: Royal Sovereign, because the oldest ship was the normal candidate for reassignment to training duty.

segments.title: How a longer First World War might produce Admirals, G3s, and N3s
segments.body: If the First World War continued toward 1920, Britain could probably complete the four Admiral-class battlecruisers. G3 and N3 would follow later. Delaying the treaty settlement until about 1924 could allow the G3s to proceed and perhaps one or two N3s as well. Completion of all four N3s requested in the question remains beyond that estimate.

evidence.note: A war lasting to about 1920 and treaty settlement delayed until about 1924 create different opportunities for the Admiral, G3, and N3 programs.

segments.summary: War continuing toward 1920 could complete the four Admirals, while delaying a naval settlement to about 1924 opens a path to G3s and perhaps early N3 construction.
segments.question: How long would the war and treaty negotiations need to last for Britain to build four Admirals, four G3s, and four N3s?
segments.answerShort: War to about 1920 could yield the Admirals, while a settlement delayed to roughly 1924 could permit G3s and perhaps initial N3s.

segments.title: Where to study interwar Royal Navy exercises and war gaming
segments.body: Phil Weir's Exeter PhD thesis on naval aviation exercises is the recommended starting point for this subject. It is available to download from the university. No single book is recommended for the Royal Navy counterpart to American interwar Naval War College gaming. Clarke's own thesis also contains relevant material, but in November 2022 he was still arranging its availability as a bound or digital work.

evidence.note: Phil Weir's Exeter thesis on naval aviation exercises and the publication limitations affecting Clarke's own thesis in November 2022.

segments.summary: No single book is offered for the Royal Navy equivalent of US Naval War College gaming, but Phil Weir's Exeter thesis provides an accessible route into naval aviation exercises.
segments.question: What was the Royal Navy equivalent of US Naval War College gaming, and what should a reader use to study it?
segments.answerShort: There is no single recommended book, but Phil Weir's Exeter thesis on naval aviation exercises is a useful starting point.

segments.title: Could European governments survive war to 1920?
segments.body: In a war lasting until 1920, Britain, the Scandinavian governments, and Spain are considered comparatively stable. France and Italy could face greater difficulty, while Austria-Hungary and Germany present more complicated cases. Germany could remain more stable than appearances suggest if major battlefield defeats were avoided. This scenario requires the late Allied advance to stall, because British Army successes intensified the German government's difficulties. The French Army was badly worn, and the American Army was still building the strength and capability needed to lead an advance. If British logistics and support had failed to sustain the offensive, the fighting could have continued much longer.

evidence.note: Conditional political survival, German stability without major defeats, and the importance of British advances, American readiness, and logistics.

segments.summary: Some European governments could survive a First World War lasting to 1920, but the scenario requires Allied advances to stall and places heavier strain on France, Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Germany.
segments.question: Could European governments survive if the First World War continued to 1920?
segments.answerShort: Some probably could, but several major powers would face growing strain, and the war lasts only if the Allied ground advance stalls.

segments.title: Bismarck's theoretical and battle rate of fire
segments.body: The NavWeaps figures quoted here give Bismarck's 15-inch guns a 26-second cycle at four degrees elevation, corresponding to a range well below 10,000 meters. A well-trained crew might reduce that cycle to twenty seconds. A separate May 1941 report gives ammunition-hoist delivery of 23-25 rounds per minute across all four turrets, approximately three rounds per gun. The same evaluation recorded two serious hoist breakdowns that caused long interruptions to ammunition supply. Bismarck expended 91 rounds during roughly thirty minutes at Denmark Strait. Firing-cycle time, hoist throughput, and ammunition expenditure during a battle measure different aspects of performance.

evidence.note: NavWeaps figures for low-elevation firing cycles, hoist delivery and failures, and Denmark Strait ammunition expenditure, with a linked German test report identified.

segments.summary: Bismarck's quoted low-elevation firing cycle and ammunition-hoist capacity were much faster than its average ammunition expenditure at Denmark Strait.
